extracted.intended_audience: ARIPO patent examiners, patent applicants and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) preparing or prosecuting ARIPO patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of patent applications under the Harare Protocol/ARIPO framework, covering claim drafting, sufficiency, support, interpretation, patentability requirements and exceptions (including computer-implemented and biotechnological inventions). Intended to direct examiners and inform applicants on compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness of claims (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that the claims should be concise refers to the claims in their entirety as well as to the individual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undue repetition of words or an undue multiplicity of claims of a trivial nature may be considered non-compliant. Claims may be objected to as lacking conciseness when unduly multiplied or duplicative; claims should not be presented in a way that obscures the matter for which protection is sought. Individual claims may be objected to as lacking conciseness if they contain long recitations or unimportant details that render the scope indefinite. The reasonable number of claims depends on the nature and facts of each case and the interests of the relevant public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of claims — avoid undue multiplicity (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of claims must be considered in relation to the nature of the invention the applicant seeks to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undue repetition or a multiplicity of trivial claims that make it unduly burdensome to determine the matter for which protection is sought may be objected to. Alternatives within a single claim should not make it unduly burdensome to determine subject matter. Identical or nearly identical claims that cover the same thing may be objected to, but small wording changes that change scope slightly should not usually be objected to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support in description (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims 'shall be fully supported by the description.' There must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope of the claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support must relate to the features of the claimed invention; vague statements or assertions without technical content provide no basis. An examiner should raise an objection of lack of support only if there are well-founded reasons; where raised, reasons should, where possible, be supported by a published document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and complete disclosure (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter of each claim must be supported by the description and drawings 'in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must enable the invention to be carried out as of the international filing date without undue experimentation. A person skilled in the art may use general knowledge to supplement the application. Reasonable trial and error is permissible, but not 'undue experimentation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to be considered in determining whether undue experimentation is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of the skilled person; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction in the application, including prior art references; (vi) amount of experimentation required. Also consider character of experimentation (routine vs beyond routine). Representative examples plus explanation of how they apply to the claim scope may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency commensurate with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of permissible generalization from examples must be judged in light of prior art; a claim should not be so broad as to go beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive the applicant of a just reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obvious modifications, uses and equivalents of described embodiments should not be questioned. Generic claims may be acceptable if there is fair support in the description and no reason to suppose the invention cannot be carried out across the claimed field. If information is insufficient to enable extension to parts of the claimed field, the examiner should invite evidence or require restriction of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of claims to disclosure (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed invention must be fully supported by the description and drawings, showing the applicant only claims what was recognized and described on the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are inconsistent with the disclosure if an essential element for function/operation is missing from the claim, or if there are contradictions between claims and description, or if the scope covers areas not recognized by the applicant. Examples: a fuel oil composition claim omitting an additive described as necessary would lack support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claiming — alternatives and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may define a feature in terms of its function even where only one example is given if the skilled person would appreciate other means to achieve that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the description conveys that a function is to be carried out in a particular way with no intimation of alternatives, then a claim embracing other means may not comply with support. Mere vague statements that other means 'may' be adopted may not be sufficient unless reasonably clear what they are and how to use them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of chemical compounds by parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization solely by parameters may be appropriate in certain cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such characterization is fully supported only when sufficient identifying characteristics show the applicant recognized and described the claimed invention at filing (e.g., partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation between structure and function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims (Rule 7(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing dependent claims that refer to more than one other claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim referring to more than one other claim should refer to them only alternatively. There is divergent practice: such claims may refer alternatively or cumulatively; multiple dependent claims cannot form a basis for other multiple dependent claims (but some authorities allow multiple dependent claims to form a basis). Examiners should follow applicable procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be interpreted in view of the description, drawings and general knowledge of the skilled person; special meanings given in the description should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be limited by examples in the description; if description gives a term a special meaning, that definition should be used for claim interpretation and the examiner should, if possible, require claim amendment to make the meaning clear in the claim wording alone. Claims should be read attempting to make technical sense and may depart from strict literal wording for that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims — equivalence to process claims (for search/examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain 'use' claims (e.g., 'the use of substance X as an insecticide') should be regarded as equivalent to process claims (e.g., 'a process of killing insects using substance X') for purposes of international search and examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'use' claims should not be interpreted as directed to the substance per se intended for use as an insecticide nor to an apparatus unless the claim indicates such. Be aware that national laws in some designated/elected States may treat 'when/whenever used' claims as improper process claims or excluded subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim defines a product in terms of the process by which it is made, the claim should be construed as a claim to the product per se possessing characteristics derived from the manufacturing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability of a product-by-process claim does not depend on the method of production; a product identical or obvious from prior art is unpatentable even if produced by a different process. Divergent practices exist as to whether anticipation requires the product to have been actually produced by that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic patentability requirements (Section 3(3) & (10) and Rule 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four basic requirements for patentability: (i) an 'invention' belonging to any field of technology; (ii) susceptible of industrial application; (iii) new; (iv) involves an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the foundational tests before considering additional implicit requirements; each must be satisfied for grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further requirements: enablement and technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the four basic requirements, the invention must be such that it can be carried out by a person skilled in the art, and must be of 'technical character' — relating to a technical field, concerned with a technical problem, and having technical features definable in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should assess technical character independently of novelty/inventive step; if no technical character, reject under Section 3(10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical progress / advantageous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Harare Protocol does not require technical progress or useful effect for patentability, but advantageous effects should be stated in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantageous effects are often important in determining inventive step and should be disclosed (Rule 6(1)(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoveries are unpatentable (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new property of a known material or article that is mere discovery is unpatentable because discovery as such has no technical effect and is therefore not an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the discovered property is put to practical use, it may constitute a patentable invention (e.g., a railway sleeper made from a material resistant to shock). Discovery of a natural substance is mere discovery unless a technical effect/use is shown (e.g., antibiotic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific theories are unpatentable (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalized scientific theories are not patentable (they are a form of discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices or processes applying the theory (e.g., semiconductor devices) may be patentable even though the theory is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical methods are unpatentable (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely abstract or intellectual methods such as mathematical methods are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine constructed to implement a mathematical method may be patentable; methods applied to produce a concrete technical result may also be patentable (e.g., filters designed using a method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic creations are unpatentable (exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic creations (paintings, sculptures, purely aesthetic aspects) are not patentable because appreciation is subjective and non-technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the article also has technical features or is obtained by a technical process, those technical aspects may be patentable (e.g., tyre tread, fabric structure, novel printing technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schemes, rules, methods for mental acts/playing games/doing business are unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract schemes (learning methods, games, business methods) are excluded from patentability as intellectual/abstract subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim specifies apparatus or a technical process (e.g., computers executing steps), examine as a computer-implemented invention as a whole; inclusion of conventional programmable apparatus requires examination for technical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programs for computers — technical character required
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs per se are among excluded items, but if the claimed subject-matter has a technical character (a further technical effect beyond normal physical interactions), it is not excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A further technical effect might be control of an industrial process, processing data representing physical entities, improving internal functioning/efficiency/security of the computer, or affecting data transfer rates. Claims should define features that assure patentability of the process the program carries out; technical considerations required to carry out the invention should be reflected in claims. Examination approach: prima facie technicality test, then assess novelty and inventive step by establishing an objective technical problem and technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentations of information are unpatentable unless technical features present
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation of information defined solely by content is not patentable, whether as presentation per se or processes/apparatus for presenting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the presentation has new technical features (arrangement or manner distinct from content), patentable subject-matter may exist — examples include specific telegraph/communication systems, measuring instruments producing particular graph forms, gramophone groove forms, data structures that inherently comprise technical features of the program operating on them, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnological inventions — definitions and patentability (Rule 7bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Biotechnological inventions' concern products consisting of or containing biological material or processes by means of which biological material is produced, processed or used. 'Biological material' means material containing genetic information capable of reproducing itself or being reproduced in a biological system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle biotechnological inventions are patentable under the Harare Protocol. Items on a non-exhaustive list are patentable: (i) biological material isolated from its natural environment or produced by a technical process even if it occurred in nature (but the human body and simple discovery of its elements are not patentable); (ii) plants or animals if technical feasibility is not confined to a particular variety; (iii) microbiological or other technical processes and products obtained by such processes. Gene sequences require disclosure of industrial application in the application as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to patentability for ordre public or morality (Section 3(10)(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any invention whose commercial exploitation would be contrary to 'ordre public' or morality is excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the public would regard the invention as so abhorrent that grant would be inconceivable (e.g., anti-personnel mines). Mere possibility of abuse is not sufficient if invention can also be used innocuously. If the application explicitly references an immoral/contrary use, deletion of that reference should be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited matter and national law differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploitation being prohibited by law/regulation in some Contracting States does not alone make it contrary to 'ordre public' or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product might be manufactured under ARIPO patent for export to States where use is not prohibited; consider national law variations before refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive vs non-offensive uses — both uses considered
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention has both offensive and non-offensive uses, refusal may be unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: process for opening locked safes — offensive use by burglar vs legitimate locksmith use. No objection arises if legitimate non-offensive uses exist. However, explicit reference to an offensive use in the application should be deleted.
